content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents an algorithm for training an ensemble of policies in deep reinforcement learning. An ensemble policy is defined as a mixture of sub-policies, and the PPO-like policy update for the ensemble policy is proposed. To control the ensemble policy behavior, the policy is updated using the KL divergence constraint on the ensemble policy. To strengthen the benefit of the ensemble policy, a regularization that encourage the diversity of the sub-policy is introduced.   The proposed method is evaluated on tasks with discrete actions. The experimental results indicate that the proposed method outperforms PPO and that the diversity regularization and the ensemble-aware loss improve the performance of the method.
content.main_review:
Strong points of the paper
- paper is well-written and easy to follow
- proposed method is clearly presented

Weak points of the paper
- novelty of the proposed method is not clear
- experimental results are not convincing enough

Detailed comments

The idea of training an ensemble of policies is not novel, and it is also common to introduce the techniques that encourage the diversity of sub-policies. For example, recent studies such as [1,2] proposed algorithms for training ensemble of polices (In [2], authors call an ensemble of policies a mixture of experts.)  Compared to these previous studies, I do not see clear significant novelty of the proposed method.

[1] K. Lee et al., SUNRISE: A Simple Unified Framework for Ensemble Learning in Deep Reinforcement Learning, ICML2021

[2] R. Akrour et al., Continuous Action Reinforcement Learning from a Mixture of Interpretable Experts, IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence (TPAMI), early access.

[3] Jack Parker-Holder et al.,  Effective diversity in population based reinforcement learning. NeurIPS 2020.

Especially, the algorithm presented in [2] also uses the PPO-like KL divergence constraints. I would like to encourage the authors to discuss the advantages of the proposed method compared with these existing methods.

The experimental results are not very convincing. I see some weak points of the experiments.
- Although the proposed method is applicable to continuous control tasks, it is evaluated on a few tasks with discrete actions. I would like to encourage the authors to evaluate the tasks on continuous control tasks as well. 

- The proposed method should be compared with more recent methods, e.g. methods presented in [1,2,3].

- Although the diversity is compared with DIAYN, DIAYN is not developed for solving a specific task. A recent study [4] proposed an algorithm, SMERL, that discovers diverse solutions using the unsupervised reward proposed in DIAYN. SMERL is more appropriate baseline for evaluating the diversity of policies.

[4] S. Kumar et al., One Solution is Not All You Need: Few-Shot Extrapolation via Structured MaxEnt RL. NeurIPS 2020.
content.summary_of_the_review: While the paper is well-written, the novelty of the proposed method is not clear. In addition, the experiments can be improved by adding continuous control tasks and more recent methods as baselines. I would like to encourage the authors to discuss the novelty of the proposed method and strengthen the experiments.

Although training an ensemble of policies [1] and introducing the techniques that encourage the diversity among the sub-policies [3] have been studied in reinforcement learning, the diversity among sub-policies is paid little attention in policy ensemble.

In our work, we introduce the diversity strengthen regularization to improve the generalization performance and encourage coordination among the sub-policies. And we are the first to apply diversity regularization on the policy space in policy ensemble to the best of our knowledge.

Moreover, we make an analysis on the reason why the policy ensemble works in RL and find that ensemble policy enjoys larger entropy which leads to better exploration and sample efficiency, which is quite different to that in ensemble supervised learning.

> **Q2. "Although the proposed method is applicable to continuous control tasks, it is evaluated on a few tasks with discrete actions."**

We will conduct experiments on MuJoCo environment, and the results will be uploaded when finished.

> **Q3. The proposed method should be compared with more recent methods, e.g. methods presented in [1,2,3].**

Thank you for providing additional methods for comparison, we will take [1,5] as our baselines.

As for baselines, we think it is necessary to add a baseline which is under the framework of the mixture of experts (MOE). However, considering that the target of [2] is to enhance interpretation and the performance is sacrificed to some extent, we take another recent work PMOE [5] recommended by reviewer qsDK, which is also under the framework of MOE, as a baseline. Finally, [3] focuses on training a population of diverse policies instead of ensemble, which is not a work on ensemble learning, thus we omit comparing with it in our setting.

In our paper, DIAYN does not serve as a baseline. And the target of the experiment about DIAYN is to show that only pursuing diversity without considering the true reward function is useless for maximizing the true rewards. Thus, we omit comparing with SMERL [4].

content.title: Response to Reviewer mGqe
content.comment:
Thanks for your insightful comments and suggestions.

> **Q1. "1.	The proposed method is actually well-known from literature, not surprising [1]."**

Directly policy ensemble [1] has been studied in the existing work, but the coordination among the sub-policies and the mechanism on why policy ensemble works is not well studied. Take [1] as an example, it just trains several policies *separately* then aggregates them without jointly training under a unified optimization objective nor considering the coordination among these policies during training.

In our method, we apply an ensemble loss to encourage the coordination among sub-policies and achieve better performance. And a diversity strengthen regularization is used to prevent the sub-policies from collapsing into a singular mode and improve the generalization performance of the policy in real-world tasks. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to apply diversity regularization on the policy space in policy ensemble. Moreover, we make an analysis on why policy ensemble works in RL and find that ensemble policy enjoys larger entropy which leads to better exploration and higher sample efficiency.

> **Q2. "The test tasks are not very challenging."**

As said in the response to Reviewer qsDK, we add the experiments on arcade learning environment which is widely used for testing the performance of RL algorithms. And the results on arcade learning environment are shown as follows:

**Evaluation scores across arcade learning environment averaged over 100 episodes using PPO as the sub-policy
at 10M interactions. Here K (the number of sub-policies) is set to 4 and all results represent the average of 5 random training runs.**

|          | PPO    | PEMV  | PEMA  | ComEns | DnC   | PMOE [3]  | DEPL    |
|----------|--------|-------|-------|--------|-------|--------|---------|
| Alien    | 1174.6 | 678   | 815.2 | 351.6  | 158   | 1488.2 | 1984    |
| Amidar   | 283.8  | 74.3  | 113.8 | 51.0   | 41.5  | 247.3  | 439.7   |
| Pong     | 20.8   | 6.9   | 7.6   | -20.7  | -21.0 | 3.0    | 20.9    |
| Seaquest | 1110.2 | 364.2 | 563.4 | 504.2  | 185   | 1800.5 | 1881.2  |

Moreover, we will conduct additional experiments on MuJoCo environment which contains several challenging continuous control tasks.

> **Q3. "For algorithmic trading, besides the two reported metrics (PA and Reward (cumulative return)), I believe many people are interested in the following trading metrics: Annual return, Annual volatility; Sharpe Ratio, Maximum Drawdown, etc."**

> **Q4. "Also for trading, some widely used comparisons are expected to include: A. Market index (benchmark performance); B. Equally weighted strategy, which is a little universal; C. Buy-and-hold, say top-20%."**

In our paper, we consider the financial order execution [2, 4, 5] scenario in financial algorithmic trading which aims at fulfilling an order within a given time horizon. But the metrics and methods mentioned are more compatible with portfolio management which targets at selecting and overseeing a group of investments that meet the long-term financial objective and risk tolerance. Due to the difference between financial order execution and portfolio management, the metrics and methods mentioned are not all suitable in financial order execution. 

Next, we will give a detailed explanation of price advantage (PA), which is the most important metric in financial order execution, and we hope the explanation can help you better understand the performance of our method. In financial order execution, we need to maximize the average execution price (AEP) for liquidation and minimize the AEP for acquirement. To present the performance of the strategy, PA, the relative gained revenue of a trading strategy compared to the AEP achieved by a common baseline strategy is computed [2]. Specifically, we take TWAP as the baseline strategy, which equally splits the order into T pieces and evenly executes the same amount of shares at each timestep during the whole time horizon. And the increasement of the PA by 1.0 can bring about a 0.5% annual return with 20% daily turnover rate (Annual return= (price advantage)×(daily turnoverrate)×(number of trading days per year)).

[4] Ning, Brian, Franco Ho Ting Lin, and Sebastian Jaimungal. "Double deep q-learning for optimal execution." arXiv preprint arXiv:1812.06600 (2018).

content.main_review:
Strength: 
* the mean aggregation method is clear and straightforward, which is wildly used in supervised-learning area. 
* The paper is well written and easy to follow. 
* Good ablation study has been done in the paper. 

Weakness: 
* the idea is simple but not novel. The mean aggregation idea is well studied in supervised learning, and it has been shown that it could provide better variance reduction of predictions. 
* To me, the entropy proof is not actually useful. Theorem 1 shows that the entropy of the ensemble policy $\hat{\pi}$ is not less than the average entropy of sub-polices. However, the reason that motivates us to use ensembled polices with regardless of its computational complexity, is if the ensembled policy could have better exploration than the usual single policy, not an average of polices. 
* Experiments are not extensive. The paper evaluates the idea on two Minigrid environments for showing better sample efficiency and one financial trading data for illustrating generalization ability. As we know, performance of RL algorithms varies over tasks. Better try to add more tasks or environments to make the empirical proof stronger, such as MuJoCo location motion tasks. 
* As stated in the paper that the idea or technique could be applied on any policy learning of RL algorithms, better try to add other methods not just PPO here, which only represents the on-policy learning algorithm. 
* From the experiment plots and tables, it seems that the proposed devesity encouraging regularization does not help much on the performance. The improvement seems incremental. 

Actionable feedback is included in the weakness part.

content.title: Response to Reviewer L5en (Part 1/2)
content.comment:
Thanks for your insightful comments and suggestions.

> **Q1. The idea is simple but not novel. The mean aggregation idea is well studied in supervised learning, and it has been shown that it could provide better variance reduction of predictions."?**

The mean aggregation of the action distributions from the sub-policies is different to supervised ensemble learning and has not been well studied in reinforcement learning. 

We make a theoretical analysis on the reason for the effect of mean aggregation in policy ensemble. In supervised learning, the mean aggregation is well studied and it could provide better variance reduction of predictions. However, reinforcement learning focuses on getting a larger cumulative reward during the interaction with the environment while supervised learning focuses on one-step prediction, which makes the mechanisms behind them different. Therefore, the conclusions or ensemble learning theories from the supervised learning cannot directly interpret and guide ensemble methods in policy ensemble. Since the discussion on why mean aggregation can work in policy ensemble is lacking, it is meaningful to explore the effect of the mean aggregation and the corresponding reasons in policy ensemble. And in our paper, we theoretically (with Theorem 1 in the paper) and empirically find that mean aggregation on policy ensemble can promote exploration of the policy when compared with the usual single policy. 

Moreover, considering that the diversity is important for ensemble learning and the diversity among the sub-policies is not seriously considered in policy ensemble, we apply a diversity strengthen regularization to ensure the diversity among the sub-policies. And as shown in the experiments in financial algorithmic trading environment, the diversity strengthen regularization has improved the generalization of policy learning, which has rarely been discussed from the view of policy generalization. We believe it also strengthens the contribution of our work.

> **Q2. The entropy proof is not actually useful. Theorem 1 shows that the entropy of the ensemble policy $\hat{\pi}$ is not less than the average entropy of sub-policies.**

The existing analysis in the paper is indeed not clearly enough, and we can give a more meaningful conclusion based on the existing proof here.
$$
E_{(\pi_1,\pi_2,…,\pi_K)}[H(\hat{\pi})]≥E_\pi [H(\pi)], \\,
\text{where  } \hat{\pi}(\cdot|s) = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k(\cdot|s),  \\,
\pi_{k},\pi∼P(\pi).
$$ 
The above result can be easily obtained by Theorem 1. And the equation holds if and only if when $K=1$ which is impossible in real practice. Thus, we can conclude that the ensemble policy has better exploration efficacy than the usual single policy in expectation and it is worthwhile to apply ensemble methods at the cost of more computational burden, especially in the environments where interaction is costly.

> **Q3. "Experiments are not extensive."**

>**Q4. "As stated in the paper that the idea or technique could be applied on any policy learning of RL algorithms, better try to add other methods not just PPO here, which only represents the on-policy learning algorithm. "**

As said in the response to Reviewer qsDK, we have added experiments on arcade learning environment and the results are shown as follows:

at 10M interactions. Here K (the number of sub-policies) is set to 4 and all results represent the average of 5 random training runs.**

| Alien    | 1174.6 | 678   | 815.2 | 351.6  | 158   | 1488.2 | 1984    |

content.title: Response to Reviewer L5en (Part 2/2)
content.comment:
> **Q5. The effect of the diversity strengthen regularization seems incremental.**

Motivated by the results in supervised learning, we think that diversity among the sub-policies can retain the ability of the ensemble policy to generalize to new states. Thus we introduce diversity strengthen regularization to improve the generalization while preventing the sub-policies from collapsing into a singular mode.

In Minigrid environment, the training and evaluation environments are the same. In financial algorithmic trading environment, training and evaluation environments are different because they are based on the stock information in different periods. So the effect of the diversity strengthen regularization on improving generalization is mainly reflected by the results on financial algorithmic trading environment. As presented in the paper, the improvement on PA and reward of DEPL over DEPL-Div are 3% and 8% averaged on two datasets. Specifically, the PA and annual return are proportional in some constraints. Thus, the improvement brought by diversity strengthen regularization is considerable.

In reinforcement learning, the generalization is not well studied and remains an important and difficult task [2]. In our paper, we combine the diversity strengthen regularization and policy ensemble to improve the policy generalization, which is not explored in the existing methods. We believe it also strengthens the contribution of our work.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper focuses on applying ensemble to policies in reinforcement learning, where the authors propose a method to train an ensemble of policies jointly. Specifically, the proposed method keeps an ensemble of N sub-policies, and determines the joint policy action distribution as the average of these N sub-policies, and the reinforcement learning agent interacts with the environment only with the joint policy. In order to further train each sub-policy, the authors also apply an importance weighted RL objective to each sub-policy. Furthermore, in order to encourage diversity within the ensemble, the proposed method uses a diversity loss term that encourages the action distributions between the sub-policies to be orthogonal. The overall loss for training the ensemble is therefore a weighted combination of these 3 losses.

The authors prove that the ensemble policy has larger entropy than the average entropy of sub-policies, and conduct experiments on two domains: grid-world environments and an algorithm trading benchmark. The experiment results suggest that the proposed method outperforms certain prior methods.
content.main_review:
Overall I think this paper is well written and proposes some interesting ideas in using policy ensemble. However I do find many limitations that need to be addressed.

Pros:

1. The paper is very well written. The overall organization of the paper is very clear and the results are easy to follow.

2. I find the ablation study in the grid world environment very informative. It tells us that the ensemble really helps.

Cons:

1. I’m not convinced about the novelty of the proposed method. The proposed method is largely a special case under the paradigm of mixture of experts ([1], [2]), where the mixture weights are uniform instead of a learned function. The mixture of experts model has also been applied to reinforcement learning before ([3]). Unfortunately, this paper does not include references to these prior works.

2. The scope of experiments of this paper is fairly limited. As an empirical paper, this paper only includes experiments on two grid-world domains and one algorithm trading domain, which I don’t believe is enough. A good starting point could be the arcade learning environment ([4]), a commonly adopted suite of environments with discrete action space that has been used in many reinforcement learning papers. 

3. The paper lacks certain important baseline comparisons. As a special case of the mixture of experts method, it is important to compare to [3]. As an ensemble method for policies, it is also important to compare to other RL methods that use policy ensembles, such as [4] and [5].


4. It is not clear to me why the orthogonal objective for increasing divergence makes sense. Two vectors in the probability simplex can only be orthogonal when they have non-overlapping non-zero components. I wonder if it makes more sense to use a divergence metric instead like in [5].

Given these limitations, I cannot recommend acceptance of this paper at its current state.


References

[1] Jacobs, Robert A., et al. "Adaptive mixtures of local experts." Neural computation 3.1 (1991): 79-87.

[2] Jordan, Michael I., and Robert A. Jacobs. "Hierarchical mixtures of experts and the EM algorithm." Neural computation 6.2 (1994): 181-214.

[3] Ren, Jie, et al. "Probabilistic Mixture-of-Experts for Efficient Deep Reinforcement Learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2104.09122 (2021).

[4] Bellemare, Marc G., et al. "The arcade learning environment: An evaluation platform for general agents." Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research 47 (2013): 253-279.

[5] Hong, Zhang-Wei, et al. "Diversity-driven exploration strategy for deep reinforcement learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:1802.04564 (2018).

[6] Lee, Kimin, et al. "Sunrise: A simple unified framework for ensemble learning in deep reinforcement learning." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2021.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is well written, but the novelty is limited as the proposed method is largely a special case of the mixture of experts method. The scope of experiments is fairly limited and the paper misses some important baseline comparison. Therefore, I cannot recommend acceptance of this paper.

Moreover, considering that [3] is a Q-learning based method, which is not compatible with PPO, thus we will not compare [3] with the PPO-based methods in the existing experiments. To take [3] as a baseline, we will conduct experiments on MuJoCo environment and take SAC as the sub-policy.

Finally, [4] encourages the policies to be different to achieve better exploration during training, which is not considered as an ensemble method, thus we omit comparing with it in our setting.

> **Q4. "4.	It is not clear to me why the orthogonal objective for increasing divergence makes sense. Two vectors in the probability simplex can only be orthogonal when they have non-overlapping non-zero components. "**

On the basis of a good ensemble policy, we hope that sub-policies can master different skills, which can retain the ability of the ensemble policy to generalize to new states. Thus, we take an orthogonal objective, which pursues extreme diversity, as the diversity strengthen regularization. 

Moreover, we have tried KL divergence in the financial algorithmic trading environment, but its performance is slightly worse than the orthogonal objective. Thus, in our experiments, we apply orthogonal objective as that in Eq. (6).

content.title: Re: Author Response
content.comment:
First I'd like to thank the authors for the detailed response. The authors address my concerns about empirical results, but my main concern about novelty and contribution still remains.

First of all, the theoretical analysis in this paper is just standard textbook result, since it follows directly from the concavity of entropy (theorem 2.7.3 in [1]). Even the specific use of this result in RL policies has been directly stated before in prior works ([2], equation 3). Hence I don't believe there's any theoretical contribution in this paper. Moreover, the use of diversity loss in a collection of policies has also been studied before ([3, 4]), even though this work uses a different form of diversity loss I don't believe this is enough contribution to merit the acceptance of this paper. Hence I'd like to keep my evaluation of the paper.
